description: Oghuz Turkic empire (1037–1194) that conquered Persia, Iraq, and Anatolia; the Battle of Manzikert (1071) opened Anatolia to permanent Turkish settlement and the subsequent loss of Byzantine Anatolia was the direct cause of the appeal to Rome that launched the First Crusade; Seljuk patronage of Persian literary culture, Nizam al-Mulk's Siyasatnameh, Omar Khayyam, defined classical Persian civilisation.

temporal.notes: Great Seljuk sultanate; smaller successor states persist longer in Anatolia and Syria

lifecycle_phases.description: Seljuks defeat Ghaznavids at Battle of Dandanaqan (1040); Tughril captures Baghdad from Buyids (1055), becomes protector of Abbasid caliph
Alp Arslan defeats Byzantine Emperor at Manzikert (1071), opening Anatolia to Turkic settlement; Malik Shah extends rule to Syria and Central Asia
Death of Malik Shah triggers succession wars; Crusaders arrive (1096); empire splits into regional sultanates

rise_factors.description: Superior Turkic cavalry and ghulam (slave soldier) system gave decisive battlefield advantage over Byzantine and Abbasid forces
Seljuks positioned themselves as defenders of Sunni Islam against the Shia Fatimids, gaining legitimacy from the Abbasid caliph

The Battle of Manzikert (1071) destroyed a Byzantine imperial army and captured Emperor Romanos IV. This single victory opened Anatolia to Turkish settlement and permanently altered the demographic balance of Asia Minor.

The Seljuks positioned themselves as defenders of Sunni Islam against the Fatimid Shia caliphate. Their patronage of Sunni scholars (including al-Ghazali) and madrasa construction restored Abbasid Sunni authority and garnered broad Islamic legitimacy.

Vizier Nizam al-Mulk's administrative reforms (Siyasatnama, 1091) professionalized Persian bureaucracy, established systematic taxation, and created the Nizamiyya madrasa network, the most influential educational institutions of the medieval Islamic world.

Seljuk governance of Persia reversed decades of Buyid mismanagement, rebuilding irrigation systems, resettling refugee populations, and reestablishing caravan trade safety. Per capita agricultural output recovered significantly under early Seljuk rule.

decline_factors.description: Iqta land-grant system created powerful regional governors; succession wars after Malik Shah permanently fragmented the sultanate
Crusader states, Fatimids, and eventually Mongols applied pressure on different fronts simultaneously

The iqta system (revenue grant to military commanders) progressively turned appointed tax-farmers into hereditary lords. By the late 11th century, iqta-holders refused to follow sultan commands, fragmenting the empire into competing Seljuk branches.

Seljuk princes routinely divided the empire among themselves at each succession, creating competing sultanates in Persia, Iraq, Syria, and Anatolia. These sub-sultanates often warred with each other rather than presenting unified responses to Crusader or Byzantine threats.
